Been on a bit of a slump lately as I walk from game to game, each one keeping my attention for a month or two before I shuffle off to the next thing on the list of shiny stuff I will absolutely play forever (I mean it this time!). I used to measure the length of time an MMO kept my attention in years, but my last five ventures back into the genre have seen me slogging off to something new in a month or two at best. I've put countless hours into wacraft 3 and starcraft brood war, thousands of hours into WoW and Guild Wars (and all of its damnable expansions), but ever since graduation and finding a job, titles just don't keep my attention like they used to.

I'm asking this question because this pattern repeated itself through most of this year-- From XCOM 2 off to Tharsis, then Blade And Soul, Black Desert, and finally Battleborn. The latter three titles have seen something that can only be described as a meteoric crash in player base-- from lively to dead during what longer-lived titles used to call their "honeymoon phase".

It's certainly possible that I've been the unfortunate victim of poor taste, but it seems to me more like a sign of a bigger change-- either within the gaming industry or within me (perhaps within the gaming community as a whole). It seems like audiences move in, judge, and move on in record time. For a lot of these games, this leads to a self-fulfilling cycle of community collapse. Matchmaking times or match quality suffer due to declining player bases, which leads to frustration or lack of satisfaction with the game, which leads to additional decline in the player base.

So what do you think? Are new games just worse than old games or is my attention span shrinking to goldfish-size?
Game Longevity -- Are games changing or am I?

Its just the reality of the industry right now. There are so many options now. Look at the music industry. Back in the day people used to listen to one record over and over. Do you think that the burgeoning number of multiplayer titles all competing for a viable community might be part of the seeming lack of longevity out of many multiplayer titles lately? If you divide even the largest community eight ways for eight games and none of them have the critical mass of players required to achieve longevity (due to matchmaking issues, let's say), it's very possible that all eight of them will die.

EDIT: going into a little more depth, we do see some companies adopting the rather successful strategy of establishing a (funded) competitive scene early in their game's life. DOTA 2 has been a huge success and Overwatch is shaping up to follow it down a similar path. This attracts highly talented streamers to essentially create free advertising for the game, which vastly improves longevity. Add the freshness and excitement of high level competitive play to that, and it almost seems obvious why games like League and DOTA do so well.

They certainly hit on something innovative with LoL and Dota. High-level competitive play, cycling character rosters, and unique and innovative (at the time it first came out) gameplay. They cracked the code to maintaining relevance despite the eventual oversaturation of the market. They also don't release a new version every year.

Overwatch is just Blizzard doing what they do. Finding a genre of games with massive potential (TF2) and making the "ultimate" version of that style game for the largest possible audience. Who knows how it will end up working out in terms of longevity...

If we go back a few years when you started to heavily get into video games there was a level of discovery that kept you interested. Remember the first time you played an FPS? The first time you played an RTS? You were probably so engrossed in it that you couldn't get pulled away. You had to learn the gameplay mechanics, the micro-ing, weapons upgrades, how to do all of that. Now that you are old and more experienced that doesn't impress you. Either those features that were new to you when you were younger are now common place or they were not added and you are wondering why they would leave out a fundamental part of the game mechanics. Now, you have a mental library of games that you can compare all new games to. And that mental library saturated your likes and expectations. Nothing is new any more. It's like the internet, once you have seen Two Girls One Cup and not gag, there isn't much that shocks you any more (as an example).

Also, as many games becomes more complex they need to equally becomes easier. For example, I remember when I played Shining in the Darkness on the Genesis, I bought graph paper to make maps as I played and after a few weeks I started to memorize the levels and know exactly where I needed to go. Today, every RPG has a map system so there is no need to remember, just hit 'm' and look at the map. Every multiplayer game is expected to have some sort of levelling system or unlockable weapons (cosmetic or functional) or some way to give the player a feeling of achievement in place of a solid story. Hack'n'Slash games used to be challenging and fun but now all feel like perpetual grindfests with hundreds of drops on every map that most of which your character can't even use because those drops are for a different class, or are impractical drops (a bat dropping a rocket launcher), or other little ticks that break immersion.

While this reply has turned more into rambling than anything, the problem you are experiencing is of a few things. You are older now, so you have a lot of experience and wisdom in games and you are starting to realise that everything you are playing today you have already played, and you are craving something new. There is also such a huge saturation in the market that the example of being hungry, opening a fridge full of food and not deciding on what to eat really plays a part here, too. When you have all the games to play you really don't have any because going back to the first point, you want something new.

As for your attention span shrinking, that seldom is the case. I have quite a lot of games in my Steam library and yet only about 8-10% of those games I actually completed. Not because of my attention span but because most of them are the same old tired games. Those that I finished have, for the most part, all had great stories that kept me interested in completing. And then there's Dota 2 which I can't seem to stop playing.
